1:
Everyone registers that a new book begins here, and none agrees how loosely its parts hang together. John Gill notes that the title is repeated because the pithy sentences begin here, the preceding chapters being a preface, and holds the sayings for the most part independent of each other, generally set in contrasted clauses and often expressed by similes. Adam Clarke goes further: it is impossible to summarise such chapters, where almost every verse contains a separate subject, and he quotes the bare note his own version was reduced to, that from here to the twenty-fifth chapter are sundry observations upon moral virtues and their opposite vices. He adds that some ancient manuscripts of the Latin head this the second book of the Proverbs. Charles Ellicott pushes back: the new title and style do mark a new collection, and each verse is complete in itself, yet the collector appears to have thrown together such as touched the same subject, though he concedes the connection is sometimes too slight to catch. Keil and Delitzsch find a different unity: the proverb about gathering in summer, standing at the head and answering to the first verse, stamps the whole as a book for youth.

Clarke alone names the form: these parallels are what a bishop of his century called the antithetic, where two lines correspond by an opposition of terms and sentiments, the degrees varying from word-for-word opposition down to a general disparity. Here every word has its opposite, father and mother being, as the logicians say, relatively opposite.

Ellicott spends his longest note on a single word. Righteousness in Hebrew is far wider than the English word: a righteous man renders to all their due, and his justice shows itself in liberality, mercy, care of speech, truthfulness, wisdom, and even consideration for animals. But since it stands here against riches got by wrong, he takes it to mean almsgiving in particular, the sense its Greek equivalent bears, the usual sense in later Hebrew, and the sense two later books give it. Gill presses the negative side, that no one can by riches redeem himself or his brother, nor put off a bodily death by one year, one day, one moment. Matthew Henry weighs it as a merchant: when profit and loss are balanced, the profit of the treasures will not countervail the loss of the wickedness, and we often see that scattered by the justice of God which was gathered by the injustice of men.

The next line divides them over one noun. Keil and Delitzsch render it not substance but craving, from a root meaning to gape, and report that the Greek and one other version wrongly found the sense of life in it while two more found possession. Ellicott independently renders it the passionate desire of the wicked, which God repels as a servant once thrust away a suppliant woman. Clarke keeps substance but adds a textual note, that twelve or fourteen collated manuscripts read not the wicked but the perfidious, a reading no ancient version acknowledges.

Over the slack hand the split reappears. Gill reports a rendering that makes it a deceitful hand, and another, from an interpreter, that makes it a deceitful balance, so that false weights would be what makes a man poor; Henry allows the deceitful hand and applies it to those who are honest only with good looking to. Keil and Delitzsch rule the balance out as contrary to biblical usage, and define the word from the body: the idea is of throwing oneself down lazily, holding oneself no longer erect with unbent muscles. Clarke states the providence flatly, that he who will not work shall not eat; Henry turns the harvest into a parable of youth, since one who idles away youth bears the shame of it in age; John Wesley reads the gathering as improving opportunities of doing good to oneself and others.
6:
One clause stands twice here, and Keil and Delitzsch read it in opposite directions. At the sixth verse they refuse the construction that makes violence the thing covered, the mouth of the wicked masking it behind words of blessing, because that renounces the sharpness of the contrast; violence is what does the covering. At the eleventh they reverse themselves: the contrast there requires violence to be the object, so the mouth of the godless hides it, and they defend the inconsistency by the manifold windings characteristic of the proverb form. Charles Ellicott arrives by the same route, noting that if the second line is taken as in the earlier verse the first must mean only that the righteous speaks to his own profit, and preferring that the mouth of the godless conceals under deceitful words the mischief meant for others. Matthew Henry makes the turn without remarking on it, stopping their mouths with shame in the first verse and having them disguise mischief with professions of friendship in the second, as one man kissed and killed and another kissed and betrayed. John Wesley supplies a custom instead of a construction, an allusion to the ancient practice of covering the mouths and faces of condemned malefactors.

A second repetition draws a variant. The closing clause of the tenth verse repeats that of the eighth, and both Adam Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch report that the Greek has something else, that he who reproves with freedom makes peace. Clarke adds two more versions and defends the sense, open reproof doing more for the peace of society than passing sin by; Keil and Delitzsch only note the striking contrast it makes with the first half.

The verse on memory gathers three of them around one Jewish usage. John Gill reports that the Jewish writers take the line as a command, let the memory of the just be blessed, and hold that whoever transgresses it breaks an affirmative precept; they abbreviate it to its initial letters and attach it to the names of their celebrated men. Keil and Delitzsch confirm the formula as the usual appendix to the name of an honoured man who has died, and Henry adopts the imperative as a duty of survivors. Clarke reads the same verse for its form, finding only two antithetic terms since memory and name are synonymous, and calls the name of the wicked as offensive as putrid carrion. He also quotes an early printed English version whose text of the sixth verse is different altogether, making the forehead of the ungodly past shame and presumptuous.

On walking uprightly Keil and Delitzsch answer a critic with chronology, the consonant text being at least five hundred years older than the accentuation his argument rests on, and explain the security simply: nothing is designedly concealed by such a man, so nothing need be feared from the light. Ellicott says the same and adds an alternative, that the crooked walker may be not found out but instructed, that is punished by misfortune. Clarke says the upright man has not two characters to support; Wesley reduces it to resting quietly on God’s providence.

Clarke reaches for anatomy at the last verse, as elsewhere in this book: the well of life is a vein of lives, an allusion to the great aorta carrying blood from the heart to every part of the body. Gill keeps the image hydraulic, a fountain continually running with wholesome water; Henry turns it agricultural, streams that water the ground and quench a weary traveller’s thirst, adding that the well is not only unpoisoned but unmuddied. Keil and Delitzsch note that where the prophets call God the fountain of life, the proverb plants the figure on ethical ground as a living power in a man. Gill takes the head of the just for Christ, and is careful to say which head of the church he means.
12:
On love covering sins Keil and Delitzsch spell out the covering: not little errors only but greater sins, covered by pardoning, concealing, excusing, or restraining them before they are executed. They separate this from the apostolic saying that resembles it, where the covering is from the eyes of a holy God, and note that neither apostle took the phrase from a Greek version. Charles Ellicott makes the same separation, judging the sense probably different, and puts the contrast crisply: hatred rakes up old feuds that had slumbered, love refuses to look at a wrong done to it. Matthew Henry keeps the covering among neighbours, love extenuating an offence as far as it can be; Adam Clarke says love pours water, not oil, upon the flame; John Gill has hatred waking contentions that were happily laid asleep.

Twice in the next two verses Keil and Delitzsch refuse constructions others adopt. At the rod they will not let it stand as a second thing found on the lips of the wise: the mouth may be called a rod of correction, but wisdom and such a rod found together would be a figure in bad taste. At the fool’s mouth they decline the reading that makes it fall in suddenly like a house, and extend the sense: it is a near, always threatening calamity, a present danger to everyone. Ellicott reaches the same phrase, since one never knows what dangerous thing such a man will say next. Clarke calls the rod a most powerful instrument of knowledge, with a lesson of profound wisdom in every twig judiciously applied. On the laying up of knowledge Gill adds that the wise hide it and do not boast of it; Clarke agrees that they keep secret whatever tends to disturb domestic or public peace, and reduces it to a rule, think much, speak little, and think before you speak; John Wesley observes that fools are more forward to lay out than to lay up.

The rich man’s strong city provokes the sharpest writing here. Clarke turns it into a protest: there is not a rich man on earth but becomes such by means of the poor, and the king himself is served of the field, so that to oppress those by whose labour all property is acquired is unjust, and diabolically so. On the other half he is bleaker, that a man in abject poverty never rises out of the pit, having no nucleus about which property may gather; he quotes a Latin poet that those rarely emerge whose exertions are cramped by want at home. Keil and Delitzsch weigh an inward reading against an outward, wealth as a consciousness of power against wealth as an actual bulwark, and judge the outward much the nearer. Henry alone makes both halves mistakes: the rich think themselves happy because they are rich, and are wrong, since wealth may expose them; the poor think themselves undone because they are poor, and are wrong too, since a man may live comfortably on little if he is content. Gill hedges too, allowing the strong city to exist in the rich man’s conceit.

At the labour of the righteous Keil and Delitzsch find the two nouns chosen with intent, one a reward of work and the other an income that need not be earned, and hold that sin carries the germ of death in itself. At the last verse they settle a point of accentuation which makes the opening word a noun, so the line reads not that a man is a wayfarer to life but that there is a way to life when one gives heed to correction. Ellicott takes the closing verb as committing error rather than causing others to err, harmonising better with the way of life just named; Henry supplies the picture of a traveller who has missed his road and cannot bear to be told of it.
18:
The first verse is read two ways. Keil and Delitzsch and Charles Ellicott both make it say that he who hides hatred is a mouth of falsehood, rather than that he hides it with lying lips; John Gill offers both, and adds that each of the two men named is a fool, the secret dissembler as much as the public slanderer. Keil and Delitzsch spend their space refusing a third possibility, the Greek reading that makes righteous lips conceal enmity; hiding hatred, they object, is a different thing from covering sin, and the Greek word for righteous is probably a corruption of one meaning deceitful. Adam Clarke leaves the grammar alone and notes how common the case is, men meditating revenge while protesting that they thought nothing of the injury.

On the multitude of words Keil and Delitzsch again reject a reading, that many words do not make a transgression cease to be what it is, since the second half calls for a general condemnation of much speaking. Gill quotes the rabbis at the same verse. Clarke states it as an impossibility to speak much and yet speak nothing but truth and injure no one’s character; Matthew Henry answers with a proverb of his own, that little said is soon amended; Ellicott says such words are sure to fail in truthfulness, or in charity, or in opportuneness.

The worthless heart draws a collation. Keil and Delitzsch report that the Greek makes it fail rather than be cheap, growing always more dejected, and object that the first half leads us to expect a designation of worth. Clarke takes it as little or nothing, or as dross, and turns sarcastic: a sinner vaunts of his heart because it is his most hidden part, and it is very honest and good, only the devil is in it.

At the next verse Ellicott offers the rendering Keil and Delitzsch have just refused. They reject making the second half say that many fools die through one demented man, since a fool has enough in his own folly and need not be drawn into destruction by others; Ellicott proposes it, arguing that as one righteous man guides many aright, so one unwise man leads many fools to ruin. Keil and Delitzsch note that the verb of the first half carries both leading and feeding. Gill denies that words feed bodies, it being not enough to bid the distressed be warmed and filled and give nothing; John Wesley says fools have not wisdom to preserve themselves, much less to feed others.

Over the blessing that makes rich, Keil and Delitzsch stand against the rest on a pronoun. The clause does not say that God adds no sorrow to his blessing, which would need a different form of the word, but that toil adds nothing to it; the proverb, they say, is a compendium of a psalm, and the first half of the old maxim about praying and working. Ellicott records both senses. Henry, Clarke and Gill all keep the sorrow, Henry defining desirable wealth as wealth held with a heart to take the comfort of it, Clarke observing that cares come with all property not so acquired and that God’s blessing levies no tax upon the comfort.

The last verse turns on one word twice. Keil and Delitzsch fix it as an outrage against morality rather than the carrying out of a plan, since all the old interpreters render it as committing a crime, and draw the elegant consequence that sin is sport to the fool and wisdom is sport to the man of understanding; Ellicott renders it exactly so. Henry notices that the word for sport is the word behind the name of Isaac, and has the fool laughing at the shaking of the spear; Clarke asks how many lies such men tell in jest, to go to the devil in earnest.
24:
The whirlwind verse turns on a single particle, and two of them read it against the versions. Keil and Delitzsch report that three old translations take it comparatively, likening the destruction of the godless to a storm rushing past, and refuse it: another word for storm would have been used, and the clause that follows differently ordered. The particle is temporal, they say: when the storm sweeps past, it is no more with the wicked. Charles Ellicott reaches the same verdict in three words, when the whirlwind passes rather than as. John Gill keeps the comparison and runs it out at length, making the whirlwind the man of sin who speaks like a dragon, the locusts of the bottomless pit, and the tyrannical persecutors who pass away suddenly, so that when the wicked perish there is shouting, most of all at the destruction of antichrist. Adam Clarke keeps the comparison too, a tornado sweeping away all before it and leaving neither branch nor root.

At the verse before, Gill reports an interpreter illustrating the fear that arrives by the builders of the tower, who feared being scattered over the earth and were scattered by the very work they raised to prevent it; he adds a second case, of men who rejected a teacher lest believing in him bring a foreign power on their city. Matthew Henry puts the principle in a line from a psalm, that as is the fear, so is the wrath: the God they provoke will prove every whit as terrible as they apprehend him to be. Clarke has the wicked getting all he dreaded, and the righteous man’s desires exceeded.

The proverb about vinegar and smoke stands out of the series, as Keil and Delitzsch note. The word properly means what is sour, but after the Greek they take it of unripe grapes, a rendering the Syriac follows and the Talmud supports. On the smoke they call two Latin poets as witnesses, one for its bitterness and one for the tears it draws. Clarke prefers chemistry, the acid dissolving the alkali of the bone until the teeth lose their texture, and the smoke irritating the tender vessels of the eye. Henry draws a professional moral: those who cannot apply their minds to business are unfit to be employed, not so much as to be sent on an errand, and therefore very unmeet to be ministers, since Christ will not own the sending of sluggards into his harvest.

The promise of long life is qualified three ways. Gill guards it at the front: it does not reach beyond the time fixed in God’s unalterable decrees, only beyond what the man expected. Ellicott guards it at the side, calling it the special blessing of the older covenant and noting that it is often fulfilled still in those who live into old age in the quiet fulfilment of duty, while others shorten their lives by anxiety or the pursuit of pleasure. Keil and Delitzsch guard it at the end, granting that the proverb has the present life in view, that the pious often die early, carried away from the face of evil or dying as martyrs, and that in such cases its verification moves forward into eternity, where the life of the pious continues and that of the godless loses itself in everlasting death. Henry alone takes it without qualification, adding that the days will be many and happy.

On the last verse Keil and Delitzsch trace both words for hope to an idea of strained and earnest looking, connected in another direction with words for strength, and correct a critic who made one of them cover fear as well: usage gives it always a joyful and never an anxious expectation. Clarke has the wicked man imposing on himself by the hope of mercy until he dies without it; John Wesley has the gladness accomplished and turned to enjoyment.
29:
The way of the Lord cuts both ways, and they say so in different registers. Keil and Delitzsch choose between the two senses the word can carry, a stronghold and a place of refuge, and take the first as the contrast demands; they observe that the way and the fear of the Lord are the two names the older covenant gives to true religion, and note that all the old interpreters render the following word as though a different form stood there. Charles Ellicott makes the sharper point: the way that protects the righteous is itself destruction to the workers of iniquity, not merely a place where destruction happens, since their rejection of the teaching of God is what condemns them. Matthew Henry allows two senses, the providence of God moving towards us or the way of godliness he appoints us to walk in, adding that the closer we keep to it the more our hearts are enlarged, and that a good conscience gives boldness in a dangerous time. Adam Clarke makes it a paradox of labour: the more the upright man works, the stronger he grows.

The verse on removal draws out the most personal writing in the chapter. Keil and Delitzsch begin from the observation that love of home is natural to everyone, then narrow it: to no people was fatherland so greatly delighted in, or banishment so dreadful a thought, as to Israel; expatriation is the worst of the evils with which the prophets threatened, and the history of the exile both confirms the proverb and explains the form it takes. Ellicott says the same and brings it forward: the godless often have to become vagabonds, as the first murderer did, and this was the punishment threatened by the lawgiver and all the prophets, which at last fell on the Jews and is still in force. John Gill lists what the righteous can be removed from — from place to place by persecution, from prosperity to adversity, from comfortable frames of soul, and at last out of this world — before naming the one thing they cannot be removed from. John Wesley allows the wicked not so much as a quiet abode on earth, much less a possession in heaven; Henry observes that they would gladly have this earth their home for ever, and cannot.

At the froward tongue Clarke turns to the criminal law, taking the threat to allude to the cutting out of tongues for blasphemy or treasonable speech, and adding that if the tongue of every scold were extracted there would soon be much less noise in the world. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch prefer botany: Ellicott has the mouth bring forth wisdom as a field brings its increase, which is why words are called the fruit of the lips, and Keil and Delitzsch set out the biblical habit of comparing thoughts to branches and words to flowers, tracing the verb to a root meaning to swell up and spring forth.

The last verse tempts an emendation and a rearrangement, and Keil and Delitzsch refuse both. A critic would change the verb, but the Greek reading offered in support is probably a corruption of another Greek word, and the version cited beside it rests on a manuscript its editor sometimes misread. The same critic would pair the halves of the two closing verses crosswise, which they grant strongly commends itself, and still decline, since the halves as they stand fit each other as contrasts. Gill draws the practical distinction that some know what is acceptable while their lips do not, being unused to saying it; Clarke observes that as the love of God is not in the wicked man’s heart, so the law of kindness is not on his lips; Wesley notes that knowledge is ascribed to the lips as elsewhere to the hands, because they are conducted by it.
